w: Dr. Litz taught this in two parts: he recorded the antibiotics half (the file is from March 2024; he gives the same lecture every year), then taught host modulation in class on Nov 5, after a quick antibiotics recap. He kept only what you need when you start treating patients. Bacteria cause it, but antibiotics are only for some cases Gum disease is started by a small group of bacteria that normally live in the mouth, mostly gram-negative, oxygen-hating rods living in a biofilm. If an exam asks what causes gum disease, the answer is bacteria and plaque ("don't even look at the other answers"). Smoking and diabetes make it worse, but without bacteria there's no gum or bone loss. Since it's an infection, antibiotics can help, but only in certain cases. Gum treatment starts with Phase I, the non-surgical part: first teaching home care (he calls it the most important visit, because nothing lasts if the patient can't keep their teeth clean), then deep cleaning (scaling and root planing), then, if needed, drugs. If antibiotics are used, they come after the deep cleaning. When antibiotics are considered: an infection that's spreading, with fever, feeling sick, or swollen glands; aggressive periodontitis, fast, severe gum disease in young people; and refractory periodontitis, gum disease that keeps getting worse even though the patient and dentist did everything right. And always as an add-on to cleaning or surgery, never by themselves. That's his main point. Why pills alone don't work: biofilm The bacteria live in a biofilm: many kinds of germs living together in a protective bubble (if one colony is a house, a biofilm is a whole neighborhood). Biofilm is sticky and won't dissolve, so rinses, water flossers and mouthwash don't remove it, just like a dirty pot left to soak still has to be scrubbed. The scrubbing is mechanical cleaning: the patient's brush and floss, and our scalers. Some biofilm germs survive drug levels 500-1000 times higher than a pill can reach. He called this one to know for life: only mechanical cleaning removes biofilm. Biofilm protects germs from antibiotics three ways: (1) it's a wall the drug can't get through; (2) it's full of beta-lactamase, an enzyme that destroys our strongest antibiotics; and (3) it slows the germs' growth, which makes many antibiotics work worse. A pill's drug spreads through the whole body, not just to the sick gum. Some reaches the gum fluid, but not enough to kill germs in a biofilm unless the biofilm is cleaned off first. Clean first, then add the antibiotic. Killers and stoppers Bacteriostatic drugs stop germs from growing and let the body finish them off. Bactericidal drugs kill germs, but only germs that are actively dividing. So if two antibiotics are given together, they must be both killers or both stoppers: a stopper would slow the germs down and leave the killer nothing to work on. Amoxicillin, and writing a prescription Amoxicillin is a penicillin that covers both gram-negative and gram-positive germs and kills them by blocking their cell walls. It's used for aggressive periodontitis. Beta-lactamase can destroy it. Dose: 500 mg by mouth three times a day for 7 days (some use 875 mg twice a day: fewer pills, so patients are more likely to take them all). Short forms: po = by mouth, qd = once a day, bid = twice, tid = three times, qid = four times. A prescription needs the drug and strength, how many to give (21 tablets for three a day for a week), and how to take it, plus the patient's details, the date, your details, refills and your signature. Allergy is the most common problem: about 10-15% of adults are allergic to penicillin. Always ask before prescribing. If they say they're allergic, ask what happens: an upset stomach is a side effect, not an allergy. Hives or trouble breathing mean a true, possibly deadly allergy: no drug from that family. Almost all antibiotics can make birth control pills work less well and can make Coumadin (warfarin), a blood thinner, too strong: they kill gut bacteria that make vitamin K, which normally blunts warfarin. You can still prescribe; just tell the patient's physician and let them decide about the warfarin. Never change another doctor's prescription yourself. Augmentin and cephalosporins Augmentin is amoxicillin plus clavulanic acid, which blocks beta-lactamase so the amoxicillin can work. It's for aggressive or stubborn gum disease. It upsets the stomach more (take it with food) and costs more. The clavulanic acid is always 125 mg. Cephalosporins work like penicillins (they kill by blocking cell walls). Newer generations cover more gram-negative germs and resist beta-lactamase better. They may reach bone better and can be taken with food. About 1 in 10 people allergic to penicillin also react to them, so don't give one if the patient is allergic to penicillin and unsure about cephalosporins. As taught, someone allergic to cephalosporins should be treated as allergic to penicillin too. Clindamycin Clindamycin blocks the 50S part of the bacterial ribosome (the machine that makes proteins) and usually kills germs. It's the usual pick when a patient is truly allergic to penicillins and cephalosporins: 150-300 mg three times a day for 7 days. Its danger is C. diff colitis: it wipes out good gut bacteria and lets C. diff overgrow, which can be deadly. Don't give it to someone who has had colitis. Tetracyclines Tetracycline stops growth by blocking the 30S part of the ribosome and covers many germs, but decades of use have made many germs resistant, so it works worse than penicillins. It may be used when A. actinomycetemcomitans is the main germ (localized aggressive periodontitis). Problems: upset stomach (most common), longer bleeding, staining and weak enamel in developing teeth (so not in pregnancy or under age 8), sunburn easily, and calcium, magnesium, iron and aluminum block its absorption: no milk, dairy, iron pills or antacids, and take it 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals. Doxycycline and minocycline are newer versions that absorb better and upset the stomach less. Doxycycline: 100 mg once a day. Minocycline: 100 mg twice a day. A tiny dose of doxycycline (20 mg twice a day) is used to block tissue-breaking enzymes (Periostat, below). Macrolides Erythromycin, azithromycin and clarithromycin block the 50S part of the ribosome and stop growth. Azithromycin and clarithromycin cover oxygen-hating germs better than erythromycin. Erythromycin isn't recommended for gum disease: too many germs resist it, and nearly everyone gets an upset stomach. Azithromycin (Z-Pak): 500 mg on day 1, then 250 mg on days 2-5; food lowers its absorption, so take it 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals. Clarithromycin: fine with or without food, but avoid it in pregnancy (pregnancy category C). Macrolides can raise levels of other drugs, especially the heart drug digoxin, and also warfarin, Dilantin, cyclosporine, midazolam, steroids and theophylline. (His story: Van Gogh's Starry Night halos may come from too much digoxin.) Metronidazole Works only on germs that can't live with oxygen, especially spirochetes. It damages bacterial DNA and kills them. Used for aggressive periodontitis and ANUG (a painful, fast gum infection), often together with amoxicillin (both killers). 250 mg three times a day. It makes warfarin stronger, can raise lithium levels, and can harm a fetus. Tell every patient: urine may turn orange-red, and no alcohol, or they'll get a terrible headache. Ciprofloxacin Cipro kills germs by blocking the enzyme that untwists their DNA (DNA gyrase). It covers gram-negative germs, but oxygen-hating germs mostly resist it, and those are the gum-disease germs. It absorbs fastest 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals, can cause sun reactions, and affects theophylline, caffeine and warfarin. It's given with metronidazole to cover the germs it misses, and only far down the list. The dose chart: know it for the exam In class he said to know the doses: "I would know this for the exam." His chart's usual adult doses, and how long to take them: Augmentin (amoxicillin plus clavulanic acid): 250 or 500 mg three times a day for 10 days. Amoxicillin plus metronidazole: 375 mg amoxicillin and 250 mg metronidazole, each three times a day, for 7 days. Clindamycin: 150-300 mg four times a day for 10 days. Doxycycline: 100 mg twice on the first day, then 100 mg a day, for 10-14 days. Metronidazole: 250 mg three or four times a day for 10 days. Minocycline: 200 mg twice on the first day, then 100 mg twice a day, for 10-14 days. Tetracycline: 250 mg four times a day for 14-21 days, the longest on the chart. The two with metronidazole aren't for children under 16, and the tetracycline family is dosed for children only over 8. A few doses differ from the drug-by-drug slides, so know both: clindamycin's slide says three times a day for 7 days, doxycycline's says 100 mg once a day, and Augmentin is usually written as 500 or 875 mg. Side effects of antibiotic pills Upset stomach and diarrhea, overgrowth of harmful germs like C. diff, weaker birth control, and more bleeding with blood thinners. To help: yogurt or buttermilk with live cultures, and an antifungal (nystatin, or one Diflucan pill at the start) for patients who get yeast infections. Drugs placed in the pocket These go into the pocket right after deep cleaning, once the biofilm is broken up. They put a high dose right where it's needed for a long time, which also lowers the chance of resistance. They can't fix the bone damage the disease already caused. When to use them: one problem spot in a patient whose gums are otherwise stable (a site that was 3 mm for years is now 5 mm and bleeding). Numb it, clean it, place the drug, and re-check in 4-6 weeks. Many deep pockets after Phase I need surgery instead. Not a replacement for cleaning, and not for aggressive periodontitis. PerioChip: 2.5 mg of chlorhexidine in a small gelatin chip that sticks when wet and dissolves on its own. The drug peaks about 2 hours after placing it and tapers off over about 9 days. Atridox: 10% doxycycline gel made by linking two syringes and mixing back and forth about 100 times (1½ minutes). It hardens in the pocket and dissolves over a few weeks. No brushing, flossing or eating at that spot for 7 days. Arestin: 1 mg of minocycline in tiny beads, squeezed into the pocket from a cartridge while pulling the tip out. It sticks when wet, dissolves on its own, and keeps working about 14 days. No brushing the spot for 12 hours and no flossing it for 10 days. Host modulation: what it means Dr. Litz taught this part in class. The host is the person the germs live on: your patient with plaque. Modulation means changing how something works in response to a trigger. So host modulation asks: can we change how the patient's body reacts to the gum germs, the reaction that causes gum and bone loss? It's taught with antibiotics because the answer involves drugs, an antibiotic among them. Germs are the key; the body's reaction is the engine Gum disease can't start or get worse without gram-negative bacteria; they're the main cause. But they're not enough on their own. He said to know this point: most of the damage comes from the body's own reaction to the germs. The deep pockets, and the bone loss on x-rays, come largely from the way our body fights the bacteria. It goes in a chain: germs build up at the gumline, the body sees them as invaders and sends cells to fight, those cells release inflammation signals (cytokines and prostaglandins), and as collateral damage the signals break down gum fibers and bone, which shows up as deeper pockets and bone loss. A deeper pocket holds more germs, more germs call in more cells and more signals, and the damage grows: a vicious cycle. But it always starts with the germs. Gum disease is not an autoimmune disease: the body doesn't attack itself for no reason. His picture is a car in your garage. The engine (the body's reaction) is what moves you from healthy gums to gum disease, but it won't start by itself in the middle of the night. It needs the key, and the key is the germs. What happens in the gum The germs: a thin saliva coating forms within minutes of a cleaning, before the patient even leaves the office, and germs stick to it. The first settlers are harmless gram-positive cocci that feed on proteins in saliva. If brushing slips, plaque at the gumline makes the gum inflamed, and that lets the nastier late germs (the orange and red complexes) move in; they feed on blood and gum fluid. The germs arrive in a set order, and the biofilm shelters them. The body's defense: first come complement proteins from the blood. They can burst germs, but their main job is to call in white cells, and they make mast cells release histamine, which makes blood vessels leaky, so the gum swells. Neutrophils are the first responders, like paramedics, arriving within about 1-2 days; if they can't win, macrophages come later. Both are good cells we can't live without, but both release cytokines, signals between cells. One cytokine, IL-1, is also called osteoclast activating factor: it switches on the bone-eating cells (osteoclasts), turns up collagenase (which breaks down gum fibers) and PGE2, and all of that releases MMPs (tissue-eating enzymes). Germs can damage tissue directly too, but how bad the loss gets depends mostly on the body's own cells. The body's reaction may be the biggest single factor in how severe the disease gets, how fast it moves, and how well it responds to treatment. Turning the reaction down, carefully Deep cleaning lowers the germ load, but it never removes every germ, especially in deep pockets and furcations. Host modulation therapy tries to turn down the destructive part of the reaction and turn up the protective part, alongside regular treatment, so the balance tips toward healing. He warned to be careful: turn someone's defenses down too far and a small infection could become serious, even deadly. Medicine already does this for arthritis and osteoporosis; dentistry started in the 1990s (Williams and Golub, 1990). NSAIDs NSAIDs (aspirin, ibuprofen) block PGE2, which turns on bone breakdown. Taken every day for up to 3 years, they slowed bone loss, but they only help if taken every day, and long-term use can cause stomach problems and ulcers, bleeding (platelets stick together less), and kidney or liver harm. So they aren't used this way. Bisphosphonates Bisphosphonates (common osteoporosis drugs, mostly for older women) slow the bone-eating cells. The problem is jawbone death (BRONJ) after an extraction or gum surgery, sometimes on its own, mostly with strong IV doses. It looks like an infection but isn't: the gum pulls back and the bone underneath dies. Treating it means scraping off the dead bone, but scraping is injury, the very thing that causes it, so the spot can come back bigger. These drugs stay in the body for years. Because of this, none is approved for gum disease. Periostat Periostat is doxycycline at a dose too low to kill germs: 20 mg twice a day, a fifth of the 100 mg antibiotic dose. It's the first FDA-approved pill for host modulation, used with deep cleaning. It blocks collagenase, the tissue-breaking enzyme made by the body's own white cells. The germs aren't affected, so they don't become resistant, and it can be taken long-term. Take it away from meals and calcium. Not for people allergic to tetracyclines, pregnant or nursing women, or children under 12. In Caton's 2000 study, patients got the same deep cleaning, then took either Periostat or a dummy pill for 9 months. Periostat gave more pocket shrinkage and attachment gain at 3, 6 and 9 months, enough to be statistically real, but only fractions of a millimeter. Don't memorize the numbers; know the point: real but small, and most useful for stubborn (refractory) and aggressive cases. Nobody has shown it works past 9 months or is safe past 12, and it never replaces cleaning and good home care. Controlling germs comes first. Periostat can be considered for people with risks that are hard to change, like smoking or diabetes, if they take it twice a day, keep brushing and flossing well, and keep coming to their gum check-ups. A pill isn't a magic cure. Bottom line Deep cleaning alone works. He said to definitely know this one: antibiotics alone don't, and they're never the first step. Added to cleaning, they can help a bit, in select cases: aggressive periodontitis, refractory periodontitis, and a few problem spots in maintenance patients. Treat the cause, not just the symptoms. His references: the Drug Information Handbook for Dentistry, the free Epocrates app, and the Little Dental Drug Booklet, which has common dental prescriptions written out.
